title: Dyeing with hops
subtitle: A warm greenish-yellow on alum-mordanted wool from spent or fresh hop flowers
excerpt: Hop flowers (cones) give a warm yellow-green on alum-mordanted wool. Spent hops from a home brew are a convenient source; fresh hops gathered at the end of summer are equally useful. The colour is soft and moderate in depth, with good light-fastness on wool.
sourceNotes: Pellew, Dyes and Dyeing (1913), Internet Archive. Hops are listed among the useful yellow-green dye plants. Hummel, The Dyeing of Textile Fabrics (1885), Internet Archive, covers the alum mordant procedure applicable here.

glossaryTerms.definition: A metallic salt used to fix plant dye molecules to wool fibre and improve colour depth and fastness.
Potassium aluminium sulphate. The standard beginner mordant for wool, giving warm, clear colours.
Resistant to fading in light. Hop-based yellows on alum-mordanted wool are moderately light-fast.

. Spent hops from home brewing (the wet cones left after boiling) are immediately usable without any further preparation. Fresh hop cones gathered in August and September give a similar result. Dried hops work but give a paler shade than fresh.

attrs.title: Mordant safety
attrs.body: Dye-pot work outdoors or in a ventilated kitchen. Dedicated pot and utensils only. Gloves and apron. Alum bath can compost after use.

attrs.title: Dye-plant cross-reference
attrs.body: Hops (Humulus lupulus) are a climbing perennial. See the Garden tutorial on growing hops for cultivation and harvest guidance.

items.name: Fresh or spent hop cones
items.qty: 2 to 3 times the dry weight of fibre

content.text: Dissolve alum in hot water and add to a pot of warm water. Enter pre-wetted wool at 40°C, raise to 80°C over 30 minutes, hold for 45 minutes. Allow to cool, remove fibre, and proceed to the dye-bath.

Pack the hop cones into the dye-pot with enough water to cover the fibre freely. Bring to 80°C and simmer for 45 minutes. Strain out the cones and return the dye liquor to the pot. Spent brewing hops may already be colour-depleted from the boiling step in brewing; if the dye liquor looks very pale, increase the hop-to-fibre ratio or use fresh cones.

Enter the mordanted fibre into the dye bath at 40°C. Raise slowly to 80°C and hold for 60 minutes, turning regularly. Let the bath cool with the fibre in it for 30 minutes. Rinse in warm water and dry in shade.

An iron after-bath deepens the yellow-green to an olive or dull khaki-green. Use as with any iron modifier: dissolve a small amount of ferrous sulphate in hot water, add to a fresh warm bath, enter the dyed fibre at 40°C, hold at 60°C for 15 minutes, rinse well. Dispose of the iron bath via the foul drain only.

items.problem: The colour from spent brewing hops is very pale or barely present
items.cause: The brewing process extracted most of the available colour from the hops, leaving little for the dye-bath
items.fix: Use spent hops at three to four times the fibre weight rather than two to three times, or supplement with fresh or dried hops. Fresh hops give significantly more colour than spent ones.

items.problem: The colour is uneven with dark and pale patches
items.cause: The dye-bath was entered too hot, or the fibre was not turned regularly
items.fix: Enter from cool and raise the temperature slowly. Turn every 15 minutes during the 60-minute dye hold.
